research_question: Do ancient Egyptian crocodile-repelling/protective formulae explicitly invoke Sobek as the controller or protector against crocodiles, or are crocodile-danger protection and Sobek cult/identity mostly parallel systems with only contextual bridges?
selection_rule: Admit texts or manuscript records only when an institutional/academic source provides a stable ancient-text identification and enough content to classify the witness without inferring from modern popular summaries. Full-text strict-overlap analysis requires an explicit translated/transliterated passage; title-only or manuscript-record witnesses are supplementary only.

witnesses.chronology: Early Middle Kingdom Coffin Text 342 antecedent; later Book of the Dead chapter 31 version in Papyrus of Nu
witnesses.source_grounded_summary: The formula explicitly commands a crocodile to back away and not approach the deceased. The surviving passage grounds protection in magical power and names of hostile beings, not in an invocation of Sobek.
witnesses.locator: UCL BD31 lines corresponding to the title and opening repulsion formula; UCL notes the antecedent as Coffin Text 342.

witnesses.chronology: Book of the Dead corpus; UCL notes three versions in Allen 1974
witnesses.source_grounded_summary: UCL's chapter index identifies Book of the Dead 32 as a formula for fighting off crocodiles. Because the full passage was not available in the audited source set, deity co-occurrence is not scored.
witnesses.locator: UCL Book of the Dead numerical index, chapter 32.

witnesses.chronology: Metternich Stela sequence; Horus-stela tradition documented from Ramesside/Third Intermediate antecedents through Ptolemaic Period
witnesses.source_grounded_summary: The formula protects a person on the water against hostile beings in the water. The Eye of Horus is explicitly part of the protective apparatus; Ra, Sekhmet, Thoth and Heka also seal or disable the aquatic adversaries. Sobek is not named in the translated passage.
witnesses.locator: UCL Horus stelae, Metternich Stela incantation 5.

witnesses.chronology: Metternich Stela sequence; formula also belongs to Horus-stela protective tradition
witnesses.source_grounded_summary: The hymn to Horus/Shed explicitly asks Horus to repel every crocodile on the river together with other dangerous creatures. Sobek is not named in the translated passage.
witnesses.locator: UCL Horus stelae, Metternich Stela incantation 10.

witnesses.chronology: Book of the Dead 88; UCL links the transformation tradition to Coffin Texts 969 and 991
witnesses.source_grounded_summary: The deceased takes the form of Sobek and claims Sobek's dread, violent seizure and reverence. The text appropriates Sobek's power; it is not a formula for repelling crocodiles.
witnesses.locator: UCL Book of the Dead chapter 88.

witnesses.chronology: Book of the Dead 113 derived from Coffin Text 158 tradition
witnesses.source_grounded_summary: Ra summons Sobek, lord of the marsh, to fish for and recover the scattered hands of Horus. This is a direct positive Sobek-Horus bridge, but it is not crocodile-repelling magic.
witnesses.locator: UCL Book of the Dead chapter 113, narrative of the powers of Nekhen.

witnesses.chronology: Middle Kingdom / Ramesseum papyrus group; British Museum describes a Middle Egyptian hymn cycle of more than 140 preserved lines
witnesses.source_grounded_summary: The British Museum identifies Papyrus Ramesseum VI as a Middle Egyptian hymn cycle to Sobek. The present gate uses the official manuscript identity as a cult witness but does not infer unverified anti-crocodile content from secondary paraphrases.
witnesses.locator: British Museum EA10759,3; Papyrus Ramesseum 6, frame 3, lines 40-58; related frames preserve the same hymn cycle.

witnesses.chronology: Surviving copies New Kingdom; composition may be Middle or New Kingdom
witnesses.source_grounded_summary: Section 7 names Sobek as child of Neith, depicts his bared teeth and immediately places him in a marsh/water-strength context. It is a positive water/power association, not a crocodile-repelling formula.
witnesses.locator: UCL Hymn to the Nile flood, section 7.

external_testimonia_control.source_grounded_summary: UCL reproduces Herodotus' report that treatment of crocodiles varied regionally: in some places they were sacred and kept/tended, while elsewhere they were treated as enemies. This is useful context but is excluded from the strict Egyptian-text overlap calculation.
